speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For the vast majority of Singaporeans, it is experienced at the bus stop downstairs, on the platform at the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) station, in the daily journey to work and back home.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It could be excellent service and smooth journeys, as articulated in the Land Transport Authority's (LTA's) Service Charter, or it can be poor service and frustrating journeys if things do not work well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ten years ago, in 2016, the figure stood at 62%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe we should instead be ambitious and aim to meet and exceed it.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To do so, our public transport network must be as convenient as, if not more convenient than, private road transport.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To that end, my speech proposes three thrusts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First, reforming the Bus Contracting Model as it approaches its 10-year anniversary to raise service standards rather than merely minimise costs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, accelerating the development of our rail network through a renewed rail financing framework and a single, publicly owned national rail operator.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Third, accelerating the roll-out of autonomous vehicles (AVs), not as a threat to employment, but as a catalyst for anchoring good jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This also comes at a time of increased public transportation demand, with new Build-To-Order projects springing up island-wide and the densification of existing Housing and Development Board estates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Commuters feel this during their daily commutes, from squeezing with other commuters on the train early in the morning to missing their bus home as it is full.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ramping up public transportation capacity is no easy feat.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Schedules need to be reshuffled, while additional buses and manpower will need to be deployed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In particular, new blood needs to be pumped into the industry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to first touch on the Bus Contracting Model.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Bus Contracting Model introduced in 2016 splits up our bus network into packages, which Public Transport Operators (PTOs) eventually bid to operate.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Aside from service quality, the LTA looks at the bid price set by the operator, which is also the service fee payable to the operator by the LTA.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The unique feature here is that the Bus Contracting Model shifted the industry from an asset-heavy framework to an asset-light contracting model, and that the Government assumed full revenue risk while operators can earn a cost-plus margin for their services.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Bus Contracting Model is a big step forward from the completely privately-run bus network of yesteryear.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Subjecting profit-motivated PTOs to a competitive tender incentivises them to keep operating costs low, which might be an issue if it adversely impacts service standards.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, is there room for us to require even higher standards on the PTOs, for the benefit of our commuters and broader public transport ridership goals?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ten years on from the launch of the Bus Contracting Model, I think it is time for us to undertake a thorough review to evaluate if the model continues to deliver good value for commuters.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have three concrete asks of the Minister when it comes to the Bus Contracting Model.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First, bus services are scheduled at headways of 15 minutes or less during the morning and evening peak periods, compared to the pre-Bus Contracting Model standard of 30 minutes or less.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From an extremely low bar of 30 minutes, we have made significant progress.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But 15 minutes is still a long time, especially if the commuter ends up not being able to board the first bus that arrives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the Government may say that we have at least half of the bus services having shorter scheduled headways of no more than 10 minutes, I believe this should not be a ceiling but a floor.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Can we aim for a shorter scheduled headway of 10 minutes or less, period?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, in a bid to spread demand out, commuters are being encouraged to travel outside of the traditional peak periods, and we ought to at least have specific schedule targets in place for off-peak periods.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On the cost side of the equation, the recent Tampines Bus Package tender results provide us with much reason to be optimistic.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This suggests that there is significant room for improvement when it comes to bus service quality.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Considering that the incumbent operator is willing to earn $50 million less and still make a profit suggests that there are significant cost savings to be made from the current expenditure levels incurred by the Government.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The latest tender award for the Serangoon-Eunos bus package on 16 July presents a similar picture, where SMRT was awarded the contract for a fee of $599.5 million and offered cost savings for LTA compared to the current contract.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Looking at the latest financials of SBS Transit, I estimate that their return on equity is 9% while their return on invested capital stands at around 18%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For an oligopolistic business, particularly where the operator takes on no fare revenue risk for buses, this appears quite high.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope that the Government can accelerate the calling of tenders for the remaining four of 14 bus packages that have never been put up for competitive tender but were instead directly negotiated between the operator and the LTA.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As the Tampines and Serangoon-Eunos examples have shown, there is significant room for cost savings and quality improvements to be made.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Third, the LTA collects Excess Wait Time, lost mileage, safety and commuter satisfaction data by operators under existing contractual frameworks.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Publishing this annually, as Transport for London does quarterly, would cost nothing additional and would allow Parliament and the public to assess the performance of operators and whether performance extensions are justified.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Most importantly, I hope that a thorough review can be conducted by the LTA, to evaluate if the model continues to deliver good value for commuters and if we can raise the bar for better public transport outcomes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our MRT and Light Rail Transit (LRT) network carries some 3.7 million rides daily, and the expansion pipeline is substantial.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Former Transport Minister Lui Tuck Yew announced all the way back in the Land Transport Master Plan 2013, that by 2030, eight in 10 households will be within a ten-minute walk of a train station.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This was again highlighted in a gov.sg Facebook post which I saw in 2020, stating, "Do you know that eight in 10 households will be within a 10 minutes' walk of a train station by 2030?" Recent commentary however seems to have shifted to the 2030s with an "s", and it gives the impression that the target has been quietly tweaked.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Regardless of whether the Government intends for this target to be reached in 2030 or 2039, if we are serious about 75% mode share by 2030 and beyond, rail is where the heavy lifting must happen.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But even as we pour tens of billions into rail infrastructure, the framework governing how our rail lines are financed and operated has become a bit of a patchwork.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The New Rail Financing Framework (NRFF) was announced under the 2008 Land Transport Master Plan, with the Downtown Line the first to come under it in 2011.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Under NRFF version one, the operator collected fare revenue and paid the Government a licence charge, bearing significant commercial risk.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: SBS Transit's North East Line and LRT lines followed in 2018, and the Downtown Line only completed its transition to NRFF version two in January 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Cross Island Line and future lines, such as the Seletar Line will, in all likelihood follow suit, with the LTA bearing all development expenditure and fare revenue risk.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, today, we have one increasingly intertwined network operating under multiple concurrent financing frameworks.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As more interchanges open and more journeys span multiple lines and operators, even more effort is expended on apportioning fare revenue between operators and reconciling different frameworks.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe that our rail network should be planned, financed and viewed holistically.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This draws on the Workers' Party's proposal in our manifesto for a National Transport Corporation: a publicly owned, non-profit entity that reinvests profits for commuters' benefit, ensures fare sustainability, optimises infrastructure revenue, attracts top talent, achieves economies of scale and enables the LTA to focus on its regulatory role.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The answer is that the right market structure follows the nature of the asset.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Buses are asset-light for the operator, the Government owns some fleet and depot assets and they can be parcelled out into distinct geographic regions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There are many capable bus operators globally; contracts turn over five to seven years; and critically as the recent Tampines bus tender showed, contestability delivers real value for money.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rail is the opposite: massive, lumpy capital expenditure over decades, deep system-specific engineering knowledge and in practice, only two incumbent operators.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Thomson-East Coast Line itself was awarded by limited tender, not open competition.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even for the Jurong Region Line, foreign operators can only participate as minority partners of SMRT or SBS Transit.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Contestability in rail is thus limited to a duopoly by design, so we should instead capture the economies of scale that a single operator brings.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Looking at foreign jurisdictions with larger rail networks than us is instructive.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Transport for London, the very jurisdiction whose quality incentive contracts inspired our own Bus Contracting Model, operates the London Underground directly through a wholly owned subsidiary while franchising its buses to private operators through competitive tender.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rail in-house, buses by tender – which is precisely the structure I am proposing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Hong Kong, the MTR Corporation operates the entire heavy rail network as a single integrated operator with on-time performance of 99%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Taipei's metro is likewise run by a single city-owned corporation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Across the jurisdictions we most often benchmark ourselves against, the single integrated rail operator is the norm and not the exception.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, Mr Speaker, we are already halfway there in practice, just not in name.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Singapore Rail Academy is also being positioned as a sector‑wide platform to build and deepen workforce competency in rail.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As with buses, I therefore have three concrete asks of the Minister when it comes to the NRFF.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, study the consolidation of rail operations into a single publicly owned national rail operator, drawing on best practices from likes of London, Hong Kong and Taipei.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Third, in the interim, publish regular updates on progress made in implementing the recommendations of the rail reliability task force.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Particular attention should be paid on the costs of the current fragmented structure and the potential synergies from network-wide harmonised data standards, pooled management of spares and supply chains, and coordinated renewal of power, signalling and trains across the network.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Frontier technologies will be critical to strengthening our economic competitiveness and anchoring good jobs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To quote the Ministry of Transport (MOT), AVs will be the next game changer.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My concern is that we appear to be more like an observer than a player in this rapidly evolving game and risk being left behind in the global push for AVs at a time when physical AI is being framed as the next wave after generative AI.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia shared in January this year, "The ChatGPT moment for physical AI is almost here" and that "Our vision is that someday, every single car, every single truck, will be autonomous".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have shared in my MOT Committee of Supply speech earlier this year, Singapore has been involved in research and small-scale testing of AVs since at least 2013.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These are 16-passenger seat vehicles in a pilot that will run for an initial three years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From a regulatory standpoint, sections 6(C), (D), and (E) of the Road Traffic Act provide a regulatory sandbox for AV trials here, with MOT's public consultation regarding an upcoming piece of legislation specific to the deployment of AV systems having just wrapped up in June.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Government's stated AV ambition, when pressed, was that Singapore would have "many autonomous vehicles" in five years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Notably, the LTA adopts a more cautious approach when implementing such technology locally, choosing to be more "calibrated and data-driven".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That is not a negative per se but let us set that against the global reality.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The AV industry in places such as China and the United States has boomed, with their biggest players – Pony AI, WeRide, Waymo and so on – already running fully driverless commercial services in the cities that they are operating in.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Amidst the growth this industry is facing, the United Nations has also introduced a regulatory framework for AVs, bridging the gap between the fragmented patchwork of regulations across different countries.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Countries in the Middle East are also showing markedly faster implementation of AVs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Dubai Autonomous Transportation Strategy aims to have 25% of the total transportation in Dubai to be autonomous by 2030.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Saudi Arabia's Transport General Authority has set a target for 25% of all goods transport vehicles to be fully autonomous by 2030.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While Singapore deliberates and conducts protracted trials, these global players and global cities are already operating at scale, creating a new ecosystem of jobs in AV research, operations and maintenance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as we have close to 100,000 private hire cars, there remains a shortage of ride-hail drivers especially during the peak periods and the wee hours of the night.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On robotaxis, as Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow has said, even if we bring all the AVs in the world to Singapore, that is less than 10% of our taxi and private hire car population.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Having AVs deployed on the specific routes and hours where the driver gap actually bites would materially help.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And the severe shortage of local bus captains presents a clear opportunity for autonomous buses to alleviate manpower pressures and satisfy rapidly growing transport demand.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A 2025 survey by the National Transport Workers' Union found that one in three public transport workers expressed concern that AVs would impact their jobs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Whether it is school buses or tour buses, operators consistently cite the challenge of driver shortages.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The shortage of local bus captains and the need to expand our public transport network is a clear and urgent impetus for us to accelerate AV deployment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is also echoed by People's Action Party Member of Parliament Mr Ang Wei Neng, who said at the debate on the Transport Motion that we need to move with a much greater sense of urgency.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, to truly anchor good jobs, we must accelerate our AV roll-out with clear, ambitious numerical targets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is not about replacing human jobs; it is about transforming the nature of work.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need to create higher-skilled roles in the AV ecosystem, from AI engineering to remote fleet management and ensure Singaporeans are trained to take up these roles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Critically, AVs should be used to grow and plug gaps in our public transport network, connecting underserved neighbourhoods with major transport nodes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would be especially helpful for those with mobility issues, such as the elderly and persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With the pilot autonomous public buses equipped with ramps for barrier-free access, I hope that the AV roll-out would be carried out with the needs of these communities in mind.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: All that is fine and good, but once again, I reiterate the question I have posed for the Minister, in that beyond stating that Singapore will have "many autonomous vehicles", in five years' time, can the MOT provide numerical targets for our AV ambition, as well as a concrete and just path towards our engagement with frontier technologies?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The three thrusts I have proposed today, a Bus Contracting Model 2.0, a unified rail financing framework and an accelerated AV roll-out with numerical targets, share a common thread: they ask the Government to organise our land transport system around outcomes for commuters, and to move quickly rather than navigate around the increasingly complex but administratively convenient structures in existence today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Indeed, for land-scarce Singapore, public transport is the most efficient and sustainable way for our people to get to where they live, work, play and study.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are committed to making mass public transport the preferred mode.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Despite these investments, we do not expect progress to be even.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our city and our people's travel needs will continue to evolve and to change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The growth of the private hire car industry has provided Singaporeans with more affordable point-to-point transport, on a pay-per-use basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: COVID-19 changed the way people travel and work, and also delayed completion of some major public transport projects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will continue to expand our public transport network to serve homes, workplaces and amenities in new areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Despite these changes, our approach is clear: we are focused on improving travel time and convenience, while putting in place the right structures and investments to ensure our public transport remains well-run and sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Like what Mr Louis Chua mentioned, to make public transport more attractive and to increase mode share, we must narrow the gap in travel time between public and private transport.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Just last week, we announced the station locations for Phase 3 of the Cross Island Line.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: When this is completed, those travelling to and from the West can save up to 50 minutes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: New lines also strengthen the resilience of our network and help relieve crowding on existing lines, improving the experience for all commuters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: While new lines are being built, we are also providing bus alternatives such as express City Direct Services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have rolled out 11 new City Direct Services since we started the Bus Connectivity Enhancement Programme in 2024, in estates like Sengkang, Punggol and Tengah.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Under this programme, we are also improving the first- and last-mile of journeys.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are providing more skip-stop feeder bus services and bus lanes to bring residents to MRT stations more quickly and reliably.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: LTA is also expanding cycling paths and adding more pedestrian-friendly features to make neighbourhoods safer and more comfortable for walking.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For these plans and programmes to be effective, they must be executed well and they must be sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We agree with Mr Chua that how we structure our public transport system to deliver well is critical.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Louis Chua has made some suggestions on the Bus Contracting Model; I would like to reiterate some key points around the Bus Contracting Model.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This has allowed us to keep the level of subsidies sustainable as we expand and improve bus services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, we tender not only to obtain better prices, but also to improve service standards and to foster innovation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The contracts are awarded based on a two-envelope evaluation process that considers first, quality and then, price.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This approach incentivises operators to deliver reliable and safe bus services, invest in their workforce and capabilities and also build expertise in emerging areas such as electrification.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: So, we should not encourage a race to the bottom based on price alone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This can cause unnecessary churn that affects day-to-day service quality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We want to assure Members that our Bus Contracting Model ensures minimum standards but does not stop us from doing better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Louis Chua gave a specific example about the wait time for buses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Before the Bus Contracting Model, the standard was to operate at intervals of 30 minutes or less and 90% of feeders ran at intervals of not more than 10 minutes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Now, more than half of the bus services run at intervals of 10 minutes or less during peak, exceeding the baseline standard of 15 minutes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Feeder buses run at even shorter intervals of eight minutes or less.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These are basic standards which operators must plan for and adhere to and we will penalise them if they fall short.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We can consider Mr Chua's suggestion to share more data on bus operators' performance over time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We must also keep in mind that more competition does not automatically resolve the real constraints we face in resources, manpower and road space.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Along the busiest corridors, we have buses arriving almost every minute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As Mr Louis Chua has shared, we face constraints on the number of bus captains we have.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have done something concrete about that – we are working with operators to attract more bus captains by raising starting salaries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But this will not change the situation overnight.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We must also be mindful that fiercer competition in bus tenders does not inadvertently affect operators' ability to pay their workers fairly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At this point, I would like to thank Mr Chua for his support for our vision to deploy more AVs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are in the process of building greater public confidence in AVs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are also increasing socialisation amongst drivers, amongst members of the public and amongst commuters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We welcome Mr Louis Chua to come by Punggol to trial the AV shuttle if he has not done so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are also working towards the AV Act, which would cover some of the questions that he has raised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I also hope that with the use of AVs, we could manage some of the manpower constraints that we have around drivers as well as bus captains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Coming back again to the bus sector, we do need to prioritise resources to areas with more urgent needs and to adjust services in response to ridership.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Louis Chua had some suggestions on rail, he suggested moving towards a single, publicly-owned national operator.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There are different rail industry models around the world, each with its own strengths and trade-offs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In Singapore, we have continued to refine our rail industry model where it makes sense to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Meanwhile, platforms like the Rail Reliability Taskforce brought our two operators together with LTA, while also engaging international experts from other metro systems to share good practices and to overcome common challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are implementing the recommendations of the Taskforce and will provide more updates along the way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Louis Chua had cited examples of overseas metros.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: LTA and the rail operators maintain good relationships with these peer systems and many others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These systems operate under different institutional and financing arrangements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We can learn from them without necessarily adopting their model wholesale.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The reality is that different sectors may require different approaches.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I think this reflects the fact that different industry structure involves different trade-offs, which must be carefully balanced and managed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling)
